```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5, dpi = 110)
```

This guide uses a single iteration of the tuna operating model to show how
vertical targeting through gear depth (hooks between floats, HBF) biases
nominal longline CPUE, and how well different standardisation models remove
that bias when the depth of the fish changes

1. not at all (**Constant**),
2. in space only (**Fixed**), or
3. in space and between years (**Moving**).

Everything else, including the seed, is identical across the three scenarios.

```{r packages}
library(cpueTargeting)
library(ggplot2)
```

# The operating model in brief

* Four species in a conceptual Southern Hemisphere ocean (north = warm):
  yellowfin (YFT) and bigeye (BET) prefer warm water, southern bluefin (BFT)
  and albacore (ALB) cooler water.
* Each species has a normal depth profile. Within each pair one species is
  shallow (YFT, ALB) and one deep (BET, BFT). A thermocline anomaly moves all
  profiles up (shallow thermocline) or down (deep thermocline).
* Hook depth follows Bigelow et al. (2002): catenary depth by HBF, with
  between-set and within-set variation and current shoaling.
* The catchability of a set for a species is the vessel's catchability times
  the overlap between hook and fish depth distributions.
* Prices favour YFT in years 1-10, BET in years 11-20 and BFT in years 21-30.
  Skippers choose where to fish and which HBF to use.

The species profiles and the expected hook profiles for each HBF:

```{r profiles, fig.height = 4.5}
plot_tuna_vertical_distributions()
```

# Step 1: define the three scenarios

The thermocline anomaly in cell *i* and year *t* is
`fixed[i] + shift[t] + annual[i, t]`, controlled by three settings:

| Setting | Meaning | Constant | Fixed | Moving |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `thermocline_sd` | SD of the fixed spatial field (m) | 0 | 30 | 30 |
| `thermocline_annual_sd` | SD of the basin-wide annual shift (m, AR(1)) | 0 | 0 | 30 |
| `thermocline_annual_field_sd` | SD of a new spatial field each year (m) | 0 | 0 | 15 |

```{r scenarios}
base <- tuna_settings()

scenarios <- list(
  Constant = modifyList(base, list(thermocline_sd = 0)),
  Fixed    = modifyList(base, list(thermocline_sd = 30)),
  Moving   = modifyList(base, list(thermocline_sd = 30,
                                   thermocline_annual_sd = 30,
                                   thermocline_annual_field_sd = 15))
)
```

# Step 2: simulate one iteration of each scenario

With the same seed, the three runs share the SST field, the fixed thermocline
pattern and the vessels.

```{r simulate}
seed <- 1
sims <- lapply(scenarios, simulate_tuna, seed = seed)
```

# Step 3: look at the thermocline

In the Moving scenario the basin-wide thermocline goes up and down between
years, and the spatial pattern changes on top of it. In the Fixed scenario
the same map applies to every year.

```{r thermocline-series, fig.height = 4}
plot_thermocline(sims$Moving)$series
```

```{r thermocline-maps, fig.height = 6}
plot_thermocline(sims$Moving)$maps
```

For comparison, the Fixed scenario (all years identical):

```{r thermocline-fixed, fig.height = 6}
plot_thermocline(sims$Fixed)$maps
```

# Step 4: why the thermocline matters for HBF

When the thermocline is shallow (orange), the deep species move up towards
the hooks of shallow sets; when it is deep (blue), they move below the reach
of all but the deepest sets. The same HBF therefore catches a different mix
of species depending on the thermocline.

```{r thermocline-effect, fig.height = 4.5}
plot_thermocline_effect(shifts = c(-40, 0, 40))
```

# Step 5: how the fishery responds

## Gear use

The fleet sets deeper gear when BET is valuable (years 11-20).

```{r hbf-use, fig.height = 3.5}
sims$Fixed$Plots$HBF + ggtitle("Fixed: proportion of sets by HBF")
```

## Vertical availability by HBF

This is the key plot. It shows the average overlap between hooks and fish for
sets with each HBF. In the Constant and Fixed scenarios the lines are nearly
flat, so an HBF factor is a good proxy for vertical availability. In the
Moving scenario the catchability of a given HBF changes from year to year with
the thermocline.

```{r availability, fig.height = 3.5}
for (sc in names(sims)) {
  print(plot_availability(sims[[sc]]) + ggtitle(sc))
}
```

## Nominal CPUE versus true biomass

Targeting through prices, location and gear depth biases nominal CPUE in all
three scenarios.

```{r nominal, fig.height = 4.5}
for (sc in names(sims)) {
  print(sims[[sc]]$Plots$CPUE + ggtitle(paste(sc, "- nominal (points) vs true (blue)")))
}
```

# Step 6: standardise each scenario

We fit the same candidate models to each scenario. `engine = "bam"` uses
`mgcv::bam(discrete = TRUE)` for speed; use `engine = "gam"` to reproduce the
guideline approach exactly.

| Model | Terms (all include `year`) |
|---|---|
| Base | year only |
| Spatial | + `s(Xobs, Yobs)` |
| DPC | Spatial + `s(PC1)` + `s(PC2)` from catch composition |
| HBF | Spatial + HBF factor |
| HBF_thermo | Spatial + HBF + `s(thermocline, by = HBF)` |
| HBS | Spatial + `offset(log(hbs_avail))`, habitat-based effective effort |

`HBF_thermo` uses the observed thermocline anomaly of the set, as an analyst
would from an ocean model. `HBS` assumes the habitat model (species depth
preferences and the HBF-to-hook-depth relationship) is known. `HBF_thermo`
cannot be fitted in the Constant scenario because the thermocline does not
vary.

```{r standardise}
models <- c("Base", "Spatial", "DPC", "HBF", "HBF_thermo", "HBS")
fits <- lapply(sims, function(sim) {
  m <- models
  if (sd(sim$Data$thermocline) == 0) m <- setdiff(m, "HBF_thermo")
  standardize_tuna_indices(sim, models = m, engine = "bam")
})
```

# Step 7: compare the indices with the truth

## Indices

```{r indices, fig.height = 8}
plot_indices(fits, models = c("Base", "HBF", "HBF_thermo", "HBS"))
```

## Accuracy

Root mean squared error of the log index relative to the true biomass trend:

```{r diagnostics, fig.height = 5}
plot_diagnostics(fits)
```

```{r rmse-table}
rmse <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(sc) {
  data.frame(scenario = sc, fits[[sc]]$diagnostics)
}))
rmse_wide <- reshape(rmse, idvar = c("scenario", "species"), timevar = "model",
                     direction = "wide")
names(rmse_wide) <- sub("rmse_log.", "", names(rmse_wide), fixed = TRUE)
knitr::kable(rmse_wide, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

## What to look for

* **Constant and Fixed**: the HBF factor should remove most of the bias,
  because the effect of HBF on catchability is the same in every year. The
  fixed spatial pattern of the thermocline is largely absorbed by the spatial
  smoother and HBF.
* **Moving**: the HBF factor should no longer be enough, especially for the
  deep species (BET, BFT). In years with a shallow thermocline, deep sets
  catch fewer deep fish and more shallow fish than average, and this shows up
  in the year effect. Models that know the thermocline (`HBF_thermo`) or the
  habitat (`HBS`) should do much better.

As a rough guide: in a prototype of this setup (seed 1, Tweedie GLMs with a
5 x 5 block factor instead of the spatial smoother), the RMSE for BET was
about 0.02-0.03 for the HBF model in the Constant and Fixed scenarios but
about 0.2 in the Moving scenario, where HBF x thermocline and HBS stayed near
0.03. Your numbers will differ. A single iteration is only an illustration;
repeat over seeds before drawing conclusions.

# Next step: interactions with year

When the effect of gear changes over time, a natural idea is to let the HBF
effect vary with time. Two versions can be added through `add_models`:

* `HBF_period`: a separate HBF effect in each 10-year price block. This tests
  whether a coarse time interaction can stand in for the thermocline. It
  cannot follow year-to-year thermocline changes, so expect little
  improvement in the Moving scenario.
* `HBF_year_re`: a random HBF x year interaction, which lets each year have
  its own (shrunk) HBF effects.

```{r interactions}
extra <- c(
  HBF_period  = "year + s(Xobs, Yobs, k = 8) + HBF_period",
  HBF_year_re = "year + s(Xobs, Yobs, k = 8) + HBF + s(year, HBF, bs = 're')"
)
fits_int <- lapply(sims[c("Fixed", "Moving")], standardize_tuna_indices,
                   models = c("HBF", "HBF_thermo", "HBS"), add_models = extra,
                   engine = "bam")
plot_diagnostics(fits_int)
```

```{r interactions-indices, fig.height = 6}
plot_indices(fits_int, models = c("HBF", "HBF_period", "HBF_year_re", "HBS"))
```

Points to keep in mind:

* With a year x HBF interaction the "year effect" is no longer unique: the
  index refers to the reference HBF (the most common level), and a different
  reference gives a different trend. Here the indices are predicted for the
  most common HBF, so if that gear is rarely used in some years the index is
  poorly informed in those years.
* A more defensible alternative is to average the predictions over the HBF
  levels (or over the fished cells and gear configurations) in each year,
  giving a marginal index, rather than conditioning on one level.
* The interaction can absorb part of the abundance signal of species that
  are caught mainly with one gear configuration. Compare the year effects with
  the truth, not only the fit statistics.
* The environmental interaction (`HBF_thermo`) explains *why* HBF
  catchability changes, so it does not compete with the year effect in the
  same way. It needs the thermocline to be observed, though.

# References

Bigelow, K.A., Hampton, J. and Miyabe, N. (2002) Application of a habitat-based
model to estimate effective longline fishing effort and relative abundance of
Pacific bigeye tuna (*Thunnus obesus*). Fisheries Oceanography 11, 143-155.

Winker, H., Kerwath, S.E. and Attwood, C.G. (2014) Proof of concept for a novel
procedure to standardize multispecies catch and effort data. Fisheries
Research 155, 149-159.
